name: Binding
first: A property wrapper that reads and writes a value that another view keeps, so that one view can change another view's state.

dependsOn.why: A binding usually reads and writes the state of another view.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The binding in `NightsEditor` reads and writes `nights`, the state of `Planner`.

dependsOn.why: A view gets a binding to its state by reading the state's projected value, with a dollar sign.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `$nights` reads the projected value of the state property `nights`, which is a binding to it.

dependsOn.why: The example writes through the binding in the closure of a modifier that runs when a view appears.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `onAppear` is a modifier of the `Text` in `NightsEditor`, and its closure adds 1 to `nights`.

what.is: A binding is a property marked `@Binding`. It holds no value of its own. Reading it reads a value that another view keeps, such as that view's state, and writing it writes that value.
what.afterExample: `Planner` keeps `nights` in state, and gives `NightsEditor` a binding to it. When `NightsEditor` adds 1 to its `nights`, the value that `Planner` keeps changes, and line 16 prints it.
what.problem: A value often belongs to one view but is changed in another, such as a number of nights that a planner keeps and an editor inside it changes. Passing the value itself would give the editor a copy, and the editor could change only that copy. A binding lets the editor change the planner's value, while the planner still keeps it.
what.how: The projected value of a state property is a binding to it, written with a dollar sign, as `$nights`. `NightsEditor` stores that binding in its `nights`. Reading or writing `nights` in `NightsEditor` reads or writes the state of `Planner`, so SwiftUI runs the `body` of `Planner` again when it changes.

when.text: Use a binding in a view that changes a value it does not keep, such as an editor. SwiftUI's own controls, such as its toggles and text fields, take a binding for the value they change.
Don't use a binding in a view that only shows a value. Pass the value itself, as a plain property, because the view never writes it.

parts.name: The binding `nights`, line 4
parts.text: The attribute `@Binding` makes `nights` a wrapped property of `Binding`, a property wrapper that SwiftUI provides. It has no first value, because it keeps no value: it reads and writes the value that the binding it is given refers to.

parts.name: The dollar sign, in `$nights`, line 17
parts.text: A dollar sign before the name of a state property reads the state's projected value, which is a binding to the state. Line 17 passes `$nights`, a binding to the `nights` of `Planner`, to the `nights` of `NightsEditor`.

steps.text: Line 21 makes a `Planner` and a renderer for it, and line 22 asks for the image, so SwiftUI draws `Planner`. Its state `nights` starts at 3.
The `body` of `Planner` runs, and line 16 prints {{Planner has 3}}.
Line 17 makes a `NightsEditor`, and gives it `$nights`, a binding to the state `nights` of `Planner`.
SwiftUI draws `NightsEditor`, and its `Text` appears, so SwiftUI calls the closure of `onAppear`. Line 8 adds 1 to the binding `nights`, which writes 4 to the state of `Planner`.
The state of `Planner` changed, so SwiftUI runs its `body` again, and line 16 prints {{Planner has 4}}.

end.text: `NightsEditor` changed the value that `Planner` keeps, through the binding that line 17 gave it.
